title: The great wave (1881–1924)
hook: Jewish families cross from Eastern Europe to America, fleeing poverty and pogroms
carry: a bundle and a folded ticket

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letter to Newport, and your line: no sanction to bigotry. Did you get a chance to hold back your nod from a cheap shot? Today, the door that letter described gets very crowded. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

A steamship ticket, folded so many times the creases have gone soft. It arrives in an envelope from America, in a small town in the Russian Empire. The one who sent it left alone, months or years ago. Worked in a shop, slept in a crowded room, saved coins in a jar, and bought passage for the next person in the family. Now that person packs a bundle, says goodbye at the edge of town, and goes. Then they save for the next ticket. Today's word is what all those tickets added up to.
screen: `A TICKET IN AN ENVELOPE.` → `ONE WENT FIRST.` → `NOW THE NEXT ONE GOES.`

segments.voice: In the years in today's title, Jews from Eastern Europe crossed to America in a great wave: from the Russian Empire, from Galicia in Austria-Hungary, from Romania and beyond. Two things pushed them. The first was poverty. Under the tsars, Jews were held to certain regions and shut out of many trades and schools, and the towns were crowded and poor. The second was the pogroms: mob attacks on Jewish neighborhoods, with homes and shops looted, and people beaten and killed, while the authorities often did little to stop them. So families worked out a plan. One goes first, then sends a ticket back. They crossed land to the ports, then the ocean, packed below deck, and came through the inspection halls at the harbor. In Yiddish, some called America di goldene medine, the golden land. The streets were not paved with gold. But there were no pogroms, and a child could go to school. The Torah has words for this kind of family story. When a farmer brought the first fruits to the Temple, he was to say a short history aloud, starting: "A wandering Aramean was my father." My ancestor wandered, went down to Egypt, lived there as a stranger, and became a people. The Passover Haggadah reads and explains that verse every year. A wanderer, a journey, a stranger who becomes a people: the great wave lived that sentence again. The years in the title end when new American laws sharply narrowed the door. By then whole neighborhoods, synagogues and newspapers had been built by people who had arrived with a bundle and a folded ticket.
screen: `POVERTY AND POGROMS.` · `ONE GOES FIRST.` · `THE GOLDEN LAND.` · `A WANDERING ARAMEAN WAS MY FATHER.` · then, large: `A WANDERER BECOMES A PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: walk your ancestors' road. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Think of your own ancestors, as far back as you can go, whatever their faith or country. Somebody made a journey, or stayed when leaving would have been easier. If you know the story, walk it in your mind: the leaving, the road, the arriving. If you don't know it, sit with the people whose names are lost but whose choices made you. If you pray, you can remember them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Goldene medine. Yiddish for the golden land, what Eastern European Jews called America as they crossed over one saved ticket at a time. Today's word.
Your line: a bundle and a folded ticket. Today, ask someone older in your family one question about where you came from, and write the answer down before it's lost. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Some Jewish families keep the stories, ship records and photographs of the ancestors who crossed, and at the Passover seder the Haggadah reads and explains the verse about the wandering Aramean.
